exEn: Food's ready!
note: Maten är klar! is how you call everyone to the table.

exEn: What do you have for breakfast?
note: äta frukost = to have breakfast; till frukost = for breakfast.

exEn: Shall we have lunch together?
note: The ch is pronounced like the sj-sound.

exEn: What's for dinner?
note: The main hot meal of the day, eaten in the evening. Often pronounced "midda".

exEn: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
note: Smaklig måltid! = Enjoy your meal!

exEn: I have a banana as a snack.
note: Literally "between-meal": a small meal like a sandwich, fruit or yogurt.

exEn: A drink is included in the price.
note: In speech people often say något att dricka (something to drink). En drink is a cocktail.

ex: Jag dricker mycket {vatten} när det är varmt.
exEn: I drink a lot of water when it's hot.
note: The e drops in the definite form: vattnet. Swedish tap water is good to drink.

exEn: We're out of milk.
note: Both the j and the l are pronounced: m-yölk.

exEn: I drink coffee every morning.
note: An ett-word (kaffet), but when ordering people say En kaffe, tack (= a cup of coffee).

exEn: Would you like tea or coffee?
note: An ett-word: teet = the tea.

exEn: Would you like juice with your breakfast?
note: Pronounced "yoos". Saft is something else: a sweet fruit cordial mixed with water.

exEn: Do you want a soda?
note: Short for läskedryck. En läsk = a can or bottle of soda.

ex: Ska vi ta en {öl} efter jobbet?
exEn: Shall we grab a beer after work?
note: En öl = a beer (a glass or bottle); beer as a drink is often ett öl, ölet. Plural öl: två öl.

ex: Vill du ha rött eller vitt {vin}?
exEn: Would you like red or white wine?
note: Wine and strong beer are sold only at Systembolaget, the state-run liquor store.

exEn: Do we have any bread left?
note: Ett bröd can be a whole loaf: Jag köpte två bröd.

exEn: Can you pass the butter?
note: The smör in smörgås (sandwich).

exEn: Can you buy cheese and milk?
note: Swedes slice cheese with an osthyvel (cheese slicer).

ex: Jag äter ett kokt {ägg} till frukost.
exEn: I have a boiled egg for breakfast.
note: Same form in the plural: två ägg.

exEn: We'll have a sandwich with our coffee.
note: Usually open-faced, with no bread on top. In everyday speech: en macka.

ex: Jag äter {gröt} med sylt till frukost.
exEn: I have porridge with jam for breakfast.
note: Usually havregrynsgröt (oatmeal), eaten with milk and jam.

exEn: Would you like yogurt or porridge?
note: Swedes also eat fil (filmjölk), a thinner sour milk, the same way.

ex: Jag äter {flingor} med mjölk på morgonen.
exEn: I eat cereal with milk in the morning.
note: Plural in Swedish: one flake is en flinga. Also called frukostflingor.

exEn: I don't eat meat.
note: k before ö is soft (the tj-sound).

ex: Vi äter {fisk} minst en gång i veckan.
exEn: We eat fish at least once a week.
note: As food, no article: äta fisk. The animal: en fisk, två fiskar.

ex: I kväll blir det {kyckling} och ris.
exEn: Tonight we're having chicken and rice.
note: k before y is soft (the tj-sound). Also means a baby chick.

exEn: The kids want sausage and mashed potatoes.
note: Korv med bröd = a hot dog, sold at kiosks everywhere.

ex: Jag tar en macka med ost och {skinka}.
exEn: I'll have a sandwich with cheese and ham.
note: sk before i is the sj-sound. Julskinka = Christmas ham.

ex: Vi äter {köttbullar} med potatis och lingonsylt.
exEn: We're having meatballs with potatoes and lingonberry jam.
note: Kött (meat) + bulle (bun). Mostly used in the plural.

ex: Vill du ha ris eller {potatis} till fisken?
exEn: Would you like rice or potatoes with the fish?
note: Stress on the second syllable. As food it is often uncountable: Vi äter potatis.

exEn: The rice needs to cook for twenty minutes.
note: Ris also means twigs, as in påskris (Easter twigs).

ex: Vi äter {pasta} med köttfärssås i kväll.
exEn: We're having pasta with meat sauce tonight.
note: Pasta med köttfärssås is a Swedish weeknight classic.

exEn: Shall we order pizza?
note: Plural pizzor, like most words ending in -a.

ex: Jag lagar {soppa} när det är kallt ute.
exEn: I make soup when it's cold out.
note: Thursday is soup day: ärtsoppa (pea soup) followed by pancakes.

exEn: I'll have a salad for lunch.
note: Also lettuce: ett salladshuvud = a head of lettuce.

exEn: You should eat more vegetables.
note: Literally "green thing". Mostly used in the plural.

exEn: I'm cutting the tomatoes for the salad.
note: Stress on the second syllable: to-MAAT.

exEn: I don't like cucumber.
note: Inlagd gurka (pickled cucumber) is a common side dish.

ex: Jag gråter alltid när jag skär {lök}.
exEn: I always cry when I cut onions.
note: Rödlök = red onion, vitlök = garlic.

exEn: The kids like eating carrots.
note: Irregular plural: en morot, två morötter.

ex: Ta en {frukt} om du är hungrig.
exEn: Have a piece of fruit if you're hungry.
note: En frukt = a piece of fruit.

ex: Vill du ha ett {äpple} eller en banan?
exEn: Would you like an apple or a banana?
note: Ett-word with the plural äpplen: två äpplen.

exEn: I eat a banana after my workout.
note: Stress on the second syllable: ba-NAAN.

ex: Kan du skala en {apelsin} åt mig?
exEn: Can you peel an orange for me?
note: The color orange is orange (said o-RANSH). Apelsinjuice = orange juice.

exEn: This pear is really good.
note: Same form in the plural: två päron.

exEn: Would you like lemon in your tea?
note: c before i is pronounced s. Stress on -tron.

ex: På sommaren äter vi {jordgubbar} med grädde.
exEn: In summer we eat strawberries with cream.
note: Mostly used in the plural. A must at midsummer.

exEn: Shall we get an ice cream?
note: False friend: glass = ice cream. A drinking glass is ett glas.

exEn: Grandma has baked cookies.
note: Usually a cookie or a plain cake. A layer cake with cream is en tårta.

exEn: I love dark chocolate.
note: ch is the sj-sound. Varm choklad = hot chocolate.

exEn: The kids get candy on Saturdays.
note: An ett-word: godiset. Lördagsgodis (Saturday candy) is a Swedish tradition.

exEn: Do you take sugar in your coffee?
note: The e drops in the definite form: sockret.

exEn: The soup needs a little more salt.
note: Also an adjective: Soppan är för salt = The soup is too salty.

exEn: Season to taste with salt and pepper.
note: The vegetable (bell pepper) is paprika.

exEn: I'm so hungry!
note: The final g is usually silent: "hungri".

ex: Är du {törstig}? Det finns vatten i kylen.
exEn: Are you thirsty? There's water in the fridge.
Mmm, so good!
note: Det var gott! = That was delicious. Comparative godare, godast (not bättre, bäst). In god morgon it simply means good.

exEn: The food at school was disgusting.
note: The opposite of god (tasty).

exEn: Fruit is good for you.
note: For food and habits; a healthy (not ill) person is frisk. General statements often use the ett-form: Frukt är nyttigt.
